name: Felix Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no tie to employers or AI firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Felix Petrov, 43, and I run a haul truck at the Kestrel Ridge mine. I check the tyres and radio before dawn, then carry ore between the loading face and crusher; the cab is quiet, but the shift wears my back out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you like, and what is life like at home after a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the route and getting a full load through without a delay. My partner Rosa works part time at a pharmacy, and our two children are still in school; the mortgage and groceries use nearly everything we bring in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the little software changes won’t empty the mine, though I wouldn’t trust every promise from management. I’d say our hourly work and the price of food matter more to my family than headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, a few automated checks might mean fewer easy tasks, but my truck still needs a person to spot a bad ramp or a loose load. I’m already stretched thin, so even a small cut in hours would land hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll keep my route and ask the shift lead what the new dispatch screen actually changes. I’ll write the hours on my pay slips down for three months and put off buying a newer phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, not frightened, because my shifts still look steady in this picture. The mortgage bill is the worry I carry before anyone mentions AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours fell by one shift, what would Rosa notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She’d see me checking the bank app before the weekly shop, and we’d skip takeout. I don’t have a spare month of bills sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your view of the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our shift board started losing names, I’d take the change more seriously. A screen that saves ten minutes is different from a manager cancelling a whole shift.

I’d say **hours** and food prices matter more to my family than headlines.
think: I think a few **routine checks** could disappear from my shift.
My **income** is already stretched, so a small cut in hours would land hard.
do: Keep my **route** and ask the shift lead what the screen changes.
Track **pay slips** for three months before buying a newer phone.
feel: I feel **watchful**, not frightened, because my shifts still look steady in this picture.

fieldNote: Felix watches his **roster** closely because even a small hours cut would strain mortgage payments.
He distinguishes a dispatch screen saving minutes from a manager **cancelling shifts**.
The delayed **phone purchase** shows how little spare cash the household has.

steps.text: Keep driving the assigned haul route
Track pay slips for three months before buying a phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that software can check plans, but the mine still needs people who know when a road is unsafe. I’d ask the union to keep an eye on staffing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office and dispatch work will change sooner than my driving, but the mine could need fewer people overall. I’m junior and there are not many similar jobs near our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my supervisor this month to show me the new AI dispatch tools during a paid shift. I’d keep working the truck and ask the union rep what happens if contractors take routes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because a smaller crew could mean fewer hours for me, even if most people remain employed. I can still ask questions and stay involved, which gives me some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children if someone at work lost a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them the adults are checking the facts and that we may need to spend carefully. I wouldn’t promise that my job is safe when I can’t know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d worry about dispatchers and the people checking orders, because those are thinking tasks the new systems can take on. Some are friends I see at the canteen.

Ask the **union rep** what happens if contractors take routes away.

fieldNote: He expects **dispatchers** to feel AI before haul drivers, yet fears a smaller mine crew.
He resists unfamiliar tools but will learn the **dispatch screen** during a paid shift.
The **union representative** gives him someone to question about contractor route cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company can’t throw out a whole crew without talking to the families first. I’d want the union and local leaders in the room before they changed the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 I’d be 45, and the thinking work would go first, then the haul trucks could be robotic around 2031. My hands-on job buys time, but not a permanent escape; few nearby employers could take me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call the union office this week and ask what income support and job advice are real, then bring Rosa to a meeting. In 2029, the first year after thinking AGI, I’d take any available shifts while we apply for support and review the mortgage with the lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed; I can picture the mine cutting my income and I already lose sleep when bills arrive. Two years is too short for me to build much of a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you try to keep current first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage comes first because the children need a home, then electricity and food. I’d speak to the lender before missing a payment, even though that call would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you call first after a layoff notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call the union representative, then Rosa, before I signed anything. I’d want someone beside me when I asked the lender about the mortgage.

I’d want the **union** and local leaders in the room.
think: By **2028** I’d be 45, and thinking work would go first.

fieldNote: The **2028 thinking shift** precedes robot trucks, but he expects lost income before 2031.
He would approach the **lender** before a missed mortgage payment and bring Rosa into planning.
Few nearby employers and a **thin cushion** make the short warning especially frightening.

steps.text: Call the union office about support and job advice
Apply for income support with Rosa in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell people five years is enough warning to make a fair plan, if the company is willing to share what it knows. I’d push the union to get a written transition offer early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48, I’d have more time than in the two-year picture, but by 2031 software could take mine planning and dispatch work. The truck work might last until robots arrive around 2034, and I still expect my hours to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union this year for a meeting about paid training and severance terms, without pretending I’ve chosen a new trade. In 2032, after thinking AGI arrives, I’d use any paid transition time to try the mine’s equipment-safety course and apply for work it actually qualifies me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but the extra three years let me ask for training before my pay is threatened. I would still worry that a short course cannot guarantee another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of training would you actually consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d consider the equipment-safety course if it is paid and leads to a named opening. I won’t sign up for a vague computer course just to feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you may try training, but dislike new technology. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still dislike learning on a screen, and I may find the course hard. I’d go because a few years of warning makes a practical try possible, not because I’m suddenly keen.

I’d push the **union** for a written transition offer early.
think: At **48** I’d have more time than in the two-year picture.
I still expect my hours to shrink before robots arrive around **2034**.

S3.quote: I won’t sign up for a vague computer course just to feel busy.
fieldNote: Five years let him seek a written **union offer** while the mine still needs drivers.

steps.text: Ask the union for paid training and severance terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years should be enough for the mine and union to agree on support before the robots reach the trucks. I’d want the town told plainly which jobs are changing and when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, thinking work is gone first, but I’d have until about 2039 before robots match hands-on work. That time helps; it doesn’t make me certain the mine will keep me until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask now for a written skills review and keep my safety record strong, while paying a little extra on the mortgage only if our bills allow it. In 2037, the first year after AGI, I’d use any course place the union secures and check local openings before deciding whether to leave the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than safe; three years between the thinking change and robot work is useful, but our thin savings still weigh on me. I can make plans earlier this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful skills review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want someone to list my truck, loading and safety experience against actual mine vacancies. If the only options require skills I don’t have, I need to hear that early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew if the mine offered a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them to ask what job it leads to before enrolling. I would take a place only if the course is paid and there is a real route into work.

I’d want the **town** told plainly which jobs are changing and when.
think: At 53, thinking work would go first in **2036**.
The **truck work** may last until robots arrive around 2039, but I’m not sure the mine will keep me.
do: Ask now for a **skills review** and keep my safety record strong.

feel: I feel **uneasy** because the robots still threaten my work and savings.

fieldNote: He wants a **skills review** tied to real mine vacancies, not a vague course promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I’d have little time before the mine could cut my work. A named paid course, a union representative in the room and clear help with the mortgage would make a difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I wish people asked what happens to the towns built around a mine when the work changes. Kestrel Ridge (the mine he works at) is not just a line on a company map; our school and shops depend on people earning wages here.

headlineQuote: Kestrel Ridge (the mine he works at) is not just a line on a company map; our school and shops depend on people earning wages here.
portrait: Felix Petrov is a 43-year-old **junior** haul truck operator with secondary school education.
His partner Rosa works part time at a pharmacy, and their two school-age children share a **mortgage** household.
**Thin savings** and few local mining jobs make even modest hour cuts a real risk.
He avoids new technology, but his plans grow more active as the AGI **warning** stretches from two to ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before the mine could reduce his income.
whatWouldHelp: A named **paid course**, union support and clear mortgage assistance would help him plan.
